meta_review.summary: This paper introduces FROND (Fractional-Order Graph Neural Dynamical Network), a novel framework for continuous graph neural networks (GNNs) that leverages Caputo fractional derivatives to capture long-term dependencies and mitigate the oversmoothing problem. Unlike traditional continuous GNNs that rely on integer-order differential equations, FROND employs fractional derivatives, which have non-local properties, allowing for a more nuanced feature update process. The authors provide a theoretical foundation for their approach, including a non-Markovian random walk interpretation of the node feature updating process. They demonstrate that the fractional order, denoted by β, can be any positive real number, offering a flexible way to control the extent of memory in the feature updates. The core idea is that by using fractional derivatives, the model can move beyond the Markovian update mechanisms of conventional integer-order models, enabling more effective graph representation learning. The paper presents a detailed theoretical analysis, including a discussion of the Caputo fractional derivative and its properties, as well as a demonstration of how FROND can mitigate oversmoothing. The authors also provide a non-Markovian random walk interpretation of the node feature updating process, which helps to understand the behavior of the proposed method. Empirically, the authors validate the FROND framework by comparing the fractional adaptations of various established integer-order continuous GNNs, such as GRAND, on a variety of datasets. The experimental results show that FROND consistently improves the performance of these baseline models, demonstrating its potential as an effective extension to enhance traditional continuous GNNs. The authors conduct experiments on node classification tasks, showing that FROND achieves better performance than the integer-order counterparts. They also perform an ablation study on the selection of the fractional order β, demonstrating that the choice of β has a significant impact on the model's performance. The paper also explores the computational cost of the proposed method, showing that it can be slower than the integer-order counterparts due to the iterative nature of the fractional solvers. Overall, the paper makes a significant contribution to the field of graph neural networks by introducing a novel approach that leverages fractional calculus to address the oversmoothing problem and capture long-term dependencies. The theoretical analysis and empirical validation provide strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed method, highlighting its potential for further development and application in various domains.
